title: Water

sections.title: Polarity, cohesion and adhesion
sections.body: Oxygen attracts shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen, so water has a partially negative oxygen and partially positive hydrogens. Its bent shape means these polar bonds do not cancel. Hydrogen bonds form between molecules. Cohesion holds water molecules together, helping a continuous water column withstand tension in xylem. Adhesion is attraction to other polar surfaces, including plant cell walls. The covalent O–H bonds within a molecule are different from the hydrogen bonds between molecules.
sections.pitfall: Evaporation separates water molecules; it does not normally split them into hydrogen and oxygen.

sections.title: Water as a biological medium
sections.body: Water surrounds ions and interacts with polar solutes, making it a medium for metabolism and transport. Non-polar substances do not dissolve readily. Water's high specific heat capacity buffers temperature changes: much of the energy supplied disrupts intermolecular interactions rather than immediately increasing temperature. Evaporation requires energy, so evaporation from a surface can cool it. Buoyancy supports aquatic organisms, while viscosity creates resistance to movement. A useful explanation links a physical property to a particular biological consequence.
sections.pitfall: A solvent is not a source of energy, and being surrounded by water does not make every substance soluble.

questions.prompt: Which interaction most directly explains cohesion in a column of xylem water?
questions.answer: Hydrogen bonds between neighbouring water molecules
distractors: Covalent bonds joining separate water molecules
Ionic bonds between every water molecule
Peptide bonds between water molecules
questions.explanation: Cohesion is attraction among water molecules. Hydrogen bonding provides this attraction; the O–H covalent bonds are inside each molecule.

questions.prompt: Explain how water can reduce rapid temperature changes in an aquatic habitat. Give two linked points.
questions.answer: Water has a high specific heat capacity.~A relatively large energy transfer causes only a small temperature change, moderating fluctuations experienced by organisms.
questions.explanation: Credit the property and its consequence. Saying only that water keeps organisms cool does not explain the mechanism.

questions.prompt: An investigation supplies 8,400 J to 100 g of water. Assume a specific heat capacity of 4.2 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ and no heat loss. Calculate the temperature rise, then state why the measured rise may be lower.
questions.answer: ΔT = Q/(mc) = 8400/(100 × 4.2) = 20 °C.~Some energy can warm the container or escape to the surroundings.
questions.explanation: Use the supplied values and units. The ideal model assumes that all transferred energy heats the water.

remaining: Overview coverage only. HL origin and persistence of water, required organism comparisons and further application practice still need dedicated lessons. Numbered references indicate relevant teaching, not certified complete coverage.

title: Nucleic acids

sections.title: Nucleotides and information
sections.body: A nucleotide contains a phosphate group, a pentose sugar and a nitrogenous base. DNA uses deoxyribose and the bases A, T, C and G; RNA uses ribose and U instead of T. Nucleotides connect through a sugar–phosphate backbone. The order of bases, rather than the backbone's repeating structure, carries sequence information. Different base sequences can therefore specify different RNA molecules and polypeptides.
sections.pitfall: A nucleotide is the whole sugar–phosphate–base unit; a base alone is not a nucleotide.

sections.title: Complementary DNA strands
sections.body: DNA usually forms a double helix with complementary bases paired between strands: A pairs with T and C with G. Hydrogen bonds hold the paired bases together; covalent bonds hold each backbone together. Complementarity makes each strand a potential template for copying the other. When calculating whole double-stranded DNA composition, the fraction of A equals T and the fraction of C equals G. This equality does not necessarily hold within one isolated strand.
sections.pitfall: Complementary strands are not identical copies of one another.

questions.prompt: Which feature distinguishes a typical RNA nucleotide from a DNA nucleotide?
questions.answer: Ribose rather than deoxyribose
distractors: A phosphate group rather than a sugar
Peptide bonds rather than covalent bonds
An amino acid rather than a nitrogenous base
questions.explanation: Both contain phosphate, sugar and base, but their pentose sugars differ. RNA also uses uracil instead of thymine.

questions.prompt: Explain why complementary base pairing allows a DNA strand to act as a template.
questions.answer: Each base pairs with a specific partner: A with T and C with G.~The sequence on the template therefore determines the complementary sequence assembled alongside it.
questions.explanation: Link the specificity of pairing to sequence copying rather than saying only that DNA has two strands.

questions.prompt: A double-stranded DNA sample contains 28% adenine. Determine the percentages of thymine, cytosine and guanine.
questions.answer: Thymine = 28%.~Cytosine and guanine share the remaining 44%, so each is 22%.
questions.explanation: A + T + C + G = 100%. The calculation applies to the full double-stranded sample, not necessarily to one strand.

remaining: Add complete molecular drawings, required evidence for DNA as genetic material, directionality and HL extensions. These two concepts do not cover every numbered understanding.

title: Origins of cells

sections.title: From chemistry to bounded systems
sections.body: Explanations of the origin of cells must account for organic molecules, a boundary, energy transformations and heritable information. Amphipathic molecules can self-assemble into membrane-like compartments, concentrating reactants and separating an internal environment from the surroundings. Such compartments are not automatically living cells. Laboratory production of organic molecules under selected conditions demonstrates chemical plausibility, but it does not establish the exact historical pathway by which life began.
sections.pitfall: Producing amino acids in an experiment is not the same as producing a living organism.

sections.title: RNA and shared ancestry
sections.body: The RNA-world hypothesis proposes that RNA played both informational and catalytic roles before the modern division of labour between DNA and proteins. Some RNA molecules catalyse reactions, supporting the plausibility of this idea. Shared features such as the genetic code and core molecular machinery support common ancestry. The last universal common ancestor is the most recent ancestor shared by all present cellular lineages; it need not have been the first life or the only organism alive at that time.
sections.pitfall: LUCA means a shared ancestor of surviving lineages, not a directly observed first cell.

questions.prompt: Which observation most directly supports the proposed dual role of RNA in an early living system?
questions.answer: RNA can contain sequence information and some RNA molecules catalyse reactions
distractors: All RNA molecules have identical sequences
RNA can function only when enclosed in a nucleus
RNA has no interactions with other molecules
questions.explanation: The hypothesis requires both a way to retain information and a way to promote reactions. Catalytic RNA is evidence of plausibility, not proof of a particular history.

questions.prompt: Explain one advantage of a membrane-like boundary for an early chemical system.
questions.answer: A boundary can concentrate reactants or maintain an internal environment.~This can increase useful interactions or allow conditions different from the surroundings.
questions.explanation: Link compartmentalization to a consequence for the chemical system.

questions.prompt: An experiment makes organic molecules using one proposed early-atmosphere mixture. A student concludes that life definitely originated through that exact mixture. Evaluate the conclusion.
questions.answer: The result supports the possibility of abiotic synthesis under the tested conditions.~It does not demonstrate that the tested atmosphere existed at the relevant place and time or that cells formed by that route.
questions.explanation: Distinguish an experimentally supported mechanism from a unique reconstruction of historical events.

remaining: Add the full sequence of required origin-of-life evidence, geological context and evaluation of alternative environments. All resources in this topic are HL-only.

title: Cell structure

sections.title: Comparing cellular organization
sections.body: All cells have a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, genetic material and ribosomes. Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus; their DNA occupies a nucleoid region. Eukaryotic cells usually have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Plant cells commonly contain cellulose walls, vacuoles and, in photosynthetic tissues, chloroplasts. Animal cells lack cellulose walls and chloroplasts. A diagram should show relative locations and label structures accurately rather than assuming that every cell has every organelle.
sections.pitfall: Not all plant cells contain chloroplasts, and a cell wall is not the same structure as a plasma membrane.

sections.title: Magnification and resolution
sections.body: Magnification is image size divided by actual size, with both measurements expressed in the same units. Resolution is the ability to distinguish nearby points as separate. Increasing magnification without increasing resolution gives a larger blur, not additional detail. A scale bar remains useful when an image is resized because the bar and image resize together. For unit conversion, 1 mm = 1,000 µm and 1 µm = 1,000 nm.
sections.pitfall: A measurement in millimetres cannot be divided directly by one in micrometres without converting units.

questions.prompt: Which structure is present in both a typical bacterial cell and a typical animal cell?
questions.answer: Ribosomes
distractors: A membrane-bound nucleus
Chloroplasts
A cellulose cell wall
questions.explanation: Both cell types synthesize proteins using ribosomes. Bacteria have no membrane-bound nucleus, and animal cells lack chloroplasts and cellulose walls.

questions.prompt: Distinguish magnification from resolution.
questions.answer: Magnification describes how much larger an image is than the actual object.~Resolution describes the ability to distinguish two nearby points as separate.
questions.explanation: Two complementary definitions are needed; increased magnification does not guarantee improved resolution.

questions.prompt: A cell is 30 mm long in an image produced at ×1,500 magnification. Calculate its actual length in µm.
questions.explanation: Divide image size by magnification, then convert the resulting unit.

remaining: Add annotated micrographs, atypical cell examples, the full range of cell structures and HL endosymbiosis and differentiation content.

title: Viruses

sections.title: Viral structure and host dependence
sections.body: A virus contains a nucleic-acid genome enclosed in a protein capsid; some viruses also have a lipid envelope. Genomes may be DNA or RNA. Viruses lack the complete cellular machinery required for independent metabolism and protein synthesis, so reproduction depends on a host cell. Attachment depends on interactions between viral surface structures and suitable host receptors, helping explain why host range is limited.
sections.pitfall: Not all viruses have an envelope, and antibiotics that target bacterial structures do not directly kill viruses.

sections.title: Lytic and lysogenic strategies
sections.body: In a lytic bacteriophage cycle, viral material enters a bacterium, host resources produce viral components, new particles assemble and the cell lyses. In lysogeny, a phage genome can integrate into host DNA and be copied with it without immediate production of large numbers of virions. Environmental changes can trigger a switch to a lytic cycle. Viral evolution involves mutation and selection, but different viruses have different mutation rates and replication mechanisms.
sections.pitfall: Lysogeny is not simply a slow version of continuous cell lysis.

questions.prompt: Why must a virus use a host cell to produce new viral proteins?
questions.answer: It lacks a complete independent protein-synthesis system
distractors: Its genome contains no information
All viral genomes are made of protein
Its capsid performs all cellular metabolism
questions.explanation: Viruses carry genetic instructions but rely on host machinery, including ribosomes, to express them.

questions.prompt: Compare lytic and lysogenic bacteriophage infection.
questions.answer: Both involve a viral genome entering and using a bacterial host.~Lytic infection produces new particles and lyses the cell; lysogeny can copy an integrated genome with the host without immediate lysis.
questions.explanation: A comparison includes a similarity and a relevant difference.

questions.prompt: A virus infects cell type X but not cell type Y. Both contain ribosomes. Suggest a testable explanation and an appropriate follow-up comparison.
questions.answer: Type Y may lack a compatible surface receptor.~Compare receptor presence or viral attachment between the two cell types while controlling viral exposure.
questions.explanation: Possessing ribosomes is necessary for host protein synthesis but is not sufficient for susceptibility to a particular virus.

remaining: Add required named-virus comparisons, viral origins and more detailed replication and evolutionary examples. All resources in this topic are HL-only.

title: Diversity of organisms

sections.title: Species and naming
sections.body: A binomial identifies an organism using a genus name followed by a specific epithet. The genus begins with a capital letter; the epithet does not. The biological species concept groups populations whose members can interbreed and produce fertile offspring, while being reproductively isolated from other groups. This concept is useful but difficult to apply to asexual organisms, fossils and some hybridizing populations. Classification should make these limitations visible rather than treating every boundary as simple.
sections.pitfall: Sharing a genus does not mean two organisms belong to the same species.

sections.title: Variation and chromosome evidence
sections.body: Members of a species vary in morphology and DNA sequence, while different species can sometimes look very similar. Chromosome number and structure provide additional evidence about organisms, but chromosome count alone does not identify a species or measure biological complexity. A karyogram arranges chromosomes so that size, centromere position and banding patterns can be compared. Conclusions about relationships are stronger when several independent sources of evidence agree.
sections.pitfall: An organism with more chromosomes is not necessarily more complex or more closely related to another organism with the same count.

questions.prompt: Which pair necessarily shares the same genus under binomial nomenclature?
questions.answer: Panthera leo and Panthera tigris
distractors: Panthera leo and Felis catus
Homo sapiens and Pan troglodytes
Canis lupus and Vulpes vulpes
questions.explanation: The first word is the genus. A shared genus does not establish that the two names describe the same species.

questions.prompt: Explain one limitation of the biological species concept when classifying fossils.
questions.answer: The concept relies on the ability to interbreed and produce fertile offspring.~Reproductive compatibility cannot normally be tested directly in extinct organisms known only from fossils.
questions.explanation: Identify the criterion and explain why the available evidence cannot directly establish it.

questions.prompt: Two species each have 24 chromosomes. A student concludes they must be each other's closest relatives. Evaluate this inference.
questions.answer: Identical chromosome counts alone do not establish closest ancestry.~Compare DNA sequences, chromosome structure and other inherited features to test the proposed relationship.
questions.explanation: A single numerical similarity is compatible with several different evolutionary histories.

remaining: Add the full set of required organism examples, genome comparisons, identification work and HL material.

title: Classification and cladistics

sections.title: Reading a cladogram
sections.body: A clade contains an ancestor and all of its descendants. A branching point represents a common ancestor; groups sharing a more recent common ancestor are more closely related on the tree. Rotating branches around a node does not change the relationships. Tip order on the page is not evidence of closeness. Branch lengths represent time or change only when the diagram explicitly supplies that scale.
sections.pitfall: An organism at the left or bottom of a tree is not necessarily primitive, and living species at the tips are not automatically ancestors of one another.

sections.title: Molecular evidence and classification
sections.body: DNA and protein sequences provide characters for comparing lineages. Shared derived features can support grouping organisms in a clade. Similar features may also arise independently through convergence, so superficial similarity can mislead. A classification can change when new molecular evidence supports a different branching history. Molecular-clock estimates depend on assumptions about rates and calibration; a count of sequence differences is not automatically an exact date.
sections.pitfall: A molecular tree is a testable inference from evidence, not an unchangeable record observed directly.

questions.prompt: Which grouping is necessarily a clade?
questions.answer: A common ancestor and all of its descendants
distractors: Any organisms with a similar body shape
An ancestor and only its largest descendants
All species living in the same habitat
questions.explanation: A clade is defined by ancestry and inclusion of all descendants, not by a chosen visible feature or habitat.

questions.prompt: Explain why classification may change after DNA-sequence evidence becomes available.
questions.answer: Similar visible traits may have evolved independently and need not indicate recent common ancestry.~Sequence evidence can support a different branching history, leading to revised groups.
questions.explanation: Link the new evidence to the purpose of a phylogenetic classification.

questions.prompt: A rooted tree has the relationship ((A,B),C). Determine which species shares the most recent common ancestor with A. Would rotating the A–B node change the answer?
questions.answer: B shares the most recent common ancestor with A.~Rotating the node changes its appearance, not the relationships, so the answer remains B.
questions.explanation: Read the branching structure rather than the order of labels across the page.

remaining: Add complete three-domain evidence, required named reclassifications and more complex tree and sequence exercises. All resources in this topic are HL-only.

title: Evolution and speciation

sections.title: Descent with modification
sections.body: Evolution is change in the inherited characteristics of populations across generations. Evidence includes the fossil record, homologous structures, patterns of DNA similarity and directly observed changes. Homologous structures share an underlying ancestry even when their functions differ. Analogous features have similar functions but can evolve independently under similar selection pressures. A robust explanation distinguishes similarity caused by shared ancestry from similarity caused by convergence.
sections.pitfall: An individual changing during its lifetime is not, by itself, a population evolving.

sections.title: Isolation and new species
sections.body: Speciation involves divergence between populations and the development of reproductive isolation. A geographical barrier can reduce gene flow. Mutation, natural selection and genetic drift can then change the separated populations in different ways. Reproductive isolation may eventually persist even if the barrier disappears. Separation does not guarantee speciation, and reproductive isolation can also arise without a new geographical barrier.
sections.pitfall: A physical barrier is a possible first step, not proof that two new species have already formed.

questions.prompt: What makes two structures homologous?
questions.answer: They derive from a shared ancestral structure
distractors: They always perform identical functions
They must look identical in adults
They evolved independently in the same habitat
questions.explanation: Homology is a statement about ancestry; functions can diverge.

questions.prompt: Explain how a geographical barrier can contribute to speciation.
questions.answer: The barrier reduces gene flow between populations.~The populations may diverge through selection, mutation and drift.~If reproductive isolation develops, divergence can persist after contact resumes.
questions.explanation: Use a causal sequence and avoid implying that every isolated population automatically becomes a species.

questions.prompt: Two isolated bird populations have different average beak sizes. Is this observation sufficient to conclude that they are separate biological species? Explain.
questions.answer: No: different average morphology can occur within a species.~Evidence of reproductive isolation or reproductive compatibility is needed to apply the biological species concept.
questions.explanation: Morphological divergence is relevant evidence but does not by itself establish the specified species criterion.

remaining: Add required named cases, timing and patterns of speciation, and HL mechanisms. This overview does not replace the complete evidence set.

title: Conservation of biodiversity

sections.title: Biodiversity and threats
sections.body: Biodiversity includes genetic variation within populations, the variety of species and the variety of ecosystems. Species richness counts species but does not describe how evenly individuals are distributed among them. Habitat loss and fragmentation, overexploitation, invasive species, pollution and climate change can reduce biodiversity. Fragmentation can isolate small populations, reducing gene flow and increasing vulnerability. A conservation assessment should specify the threat, the affected population and the evidence of change.
sections.pitfall: Counting many individuals of one species is not the same as recording high species richness.

sections.title: Evaluating conservation actions
sections.body: In situ conservation protects organisms in their habitats; ex situ conservation maintains them outside their natural habitats, for example in seed banks or managed breeding programmes. Habitat protection preserves interactions that isolated captive populations cannot reproduce. Ex situ methods can protect genetic material or support reintroduction, but require attention to genetic diversity and survival in the wild. Success should be assessed with repeated population or habitat measurements and the participation of relevant local communities.
sections.pitfall: A growing captive population alone does not demonstrate that a wild population is recovering.

questions.prompt: What does species richness measure?
questions.answer: The number of species present
distractors: The total number of individuals present
The mean body mass of organisms
The proportion of organisms in the largest species
questions.explanation: Richness counts distinct species. Abundance and evenness describe different features of the community.

questions.prompt: Compare in situ and ex situ conservation, giving one example of each.
questions.answer: In situ conservation protects organisms within their habitat, such as protecting a breeding wetland.~Ex situ conservation maintains organisms or genetic material outside the natural habitat, such as a seed bank.~Both can contribute to conserving biodiversity but preserve different aspects of it.
questions.explanation: State the location distinction and make each example consistent with the definition.

questions.prompt: After a reserve is established, surveys record 80, 96 and 112 individuals over three years. Explain why the increase is encouraging but insufficient to prove the reserve caused recovery.
questions.answer: The recorded population has increased, consistent with recovery.~Survey effort, detectability, immigration or other environmental changes could also explain the trend.~Standardized monitoring and a suitable comparison would strengthen causal inference.
questions.explanation: Separate description of the observed trend from evidence for its cause.

remaining: Add required extinction and conservation case studies, detailed biodiversity measurement and the full range of conservation trade-offs.
